1:
Everyone stops at the first clause, and each hears something different. Spurgeon presses the possessive, then the copula: "here is personal interest, my light, my salvation" — and "it is not said merely that the Lord gives light, but that he is light; nor that he gives salvation, but that he is salvation." Light comes first in experience: "where there is not enough light to see our own darkness and to long for the Lord Jesus, there is no evidence of salvation"; and "salvation finds us in the dark, but it does not leave us there." Henry hears a borrowed quality: David's subjects called him the light of Israel, but "he owns that he shone, as the moon does, with a borrowed light". Wesley reduces it to office — "my counsellor in all my difficulties, and my comforter and deliverer in all my distresses" — and Gill refers it to Christ, "the light of the world".

Ellicott places the phrase historically and traces its enlargement. The thought "appears nowhere else so grandly"; the Vulgate's rendering became the motto of Oxford. To the psalmist "Jehovah was the guiding and cheering beacon-fire, proclaiming his victory"; from that to God as the source "both of moral and intellectual light, is a long but glorious stage". He corrects the second noun as well: not strength but "defence or bulwark".

Augustine reads it as a catechumen's speech — "Christ's young soldier speaketh, on his coming to the faith" — and turns the devouring of flesh into a benefit: the guilty come near "that with their reviling tooth they may consume not me, but rather my fleshly desires." He distinguishes those "blaming me with a friendly intent" from the enemies proper.

Whether the eaters are soldiers or slanderers Ellicott decides on context: Job "would allow us to understand those who eat up flesh, as a figure for calumniators; but the context marks out the situation so clearly as that of a warrior". Clarke sets it at a battle where "the Philistine lost his own life". On "in this will I be confident" Ellicott lays out the referents without choosing — the circumstance, or in spite of it; the Greek pointing forward; the rabbis back to the opening, "that Jehovah is my light".

The occasion divides them as it did in Psalm 51. Delitzsch hears "the same longing after Zion" as the psalm before, and notes that the sanctuary is at present only a tent though called a palace "on account of Him who sits enthroned therein". Calvin has David rehearsing "the desires and meditations with which he had exercised himself in the midst of his great dangers", the thanksgivings showing it "was composed after his deliverance". Clarke allows the Davidic reading, then leans away: the words "more naturally belong to the captivity... the earnest longing of the captives to return to their own land"; at verse 6 he makes it a national hope — "we shall most assuredly be redeemed from this captivity".

On the one thing desired Spurgeon draws the moral: "divided aims tend to distraction, weakness, disappointment. The man of one book is eminent, the man of one pursuit is successful." He defends desire as such — "what we cannot at once attain, it is well to desire. God judges us very much by the desire of our hearts" — since "he who rides a lame horse is not blamed by his master for want of speed." Ellicott renders the beholding as meditation, and resists those "who would entirely spiritualise the wish, as if the actual attendance on the House of God were not in the poet's thoughts". Clarke expounds the pavilion literally, deriving the English word from the butterfly the tent resembles. Wesley hears "the ancient custom of offenders, who used to flee to the tabernacle or altar". Delitzsch takes the sacrifices of shouting as private thank-offerings, not the congregation's trumpet-blown ones.
7:
The change of key at verse 7 is noticed by everyone and explained three ways. Ellicott takes it as evidence of composite authorship: "the change of tone so marked here, from the warlike to the plaintive, leads to the supposition that" these verses "are interpolated from another song of quite another kind in contents, art, and period." Delitzsch accounts for it psychologically. Vows of thanksgiving usually close a psalm, "but in this Psalm the prayer is only just beginning at this stage"; the transition comes from the thought of surrounding danger, so that "the reality, which, in the first part, is overcome and surmounted by his faith, makes itself consciously felt here." Spurgeon puts the movement in a figure: "the pendulum of spirituality swings from prayer to praise. The voice which in the last verse was tuned to music is here turned to crying." Henry keeps it circumstantial: if David "cannot now go up to the house of the Lord, yet, wherever he is, he can find a way to the throne of grace by prayer."

Spurgeon defends the audible voice as useful though unnecessary, since it "aids in preventing distractions", and marks true prayer: "Pharisees care not a fig for the Lord's hearing them, so long as they are heard of men; but with a genuine man, the Lord's ear is everything." Clarke turns it into a rebuke: to be heard when one cries "is the utmost that any man of common sense can expect", yet "there are multitudes who suppose God will bless them whether they cry or not". Henry grounds the expectation not in merit but in "God's goodness", adding that it is "presumption for us to come into the presence of the King of kings uncalled". Gill allows that God sometimes "seems to turn a deaf ear... yet he always shows himself a God hearing prayer."

Verse 8 is where the translations part company. Ellicott says the margin "rightly rejects" the received words and "restores the order of the Hebrew", though the Authorised text "really gives its meaning". Clarke is far more drastic. He observes how much "labor and skill have been employed to make sense of this verse as it stands in our translation", from which the English "has been forcibly extracted", and renders it with the heart addressed rather than speaking: "Unto thee, my heart, he hath said, Seek ye my face." He then paraphrases it corporately, God saying to his Church, seek ye my face. Gill expounds the seeking instead: "to seek the Lord himself, and communion with him through Christ", not "bare attendance without it".

On the hidden face Ellicott makes one of his shortest notes and Clarke one of his longest. Ellicott dismisses a single word: "far" is "unnecessary and misleading". Gill notes that the hiding "is consistent with the everlasting and unchangeable love of God to his people", though "they are ready to impute it to wrath". Clarke collects Persian parallels for the turning of faces: "our face is towards Thee in all our ways; Thy face is towards us in all our intentions". Wesley reads the putting away as exclusion "from thy face or presence, or from the place of thy worship".

Verse 10 divides on whether the forsaking is real. Clarke takes the Hebrew as past and factual: "for my father and my mother have forsaken me; but the Lord hath gathered me up. My parents were my protectors for a time; but the Lord has been my Protector always." Gill denies any literal reference — not Jesse's household, nor the anointing, nor the flight from Saul — reading it "of something supposed yet to come", the parents standing for "his nearest and dearest friends, his closest adherents". Delitzsch moves past the question to the petition, picturing the psalmist "wandering about like a hunted deer" whom God "is able to guide... so that he may escape all dangers".
11:
The petition for teaching is read as submission, not information. Clarke asks that God "let me know the gracious designs of thy providence towards me, that my heart may submit to thy will", and takes the plain path as "the path of righteousness". Wesley supplies the double motive: that David may "neither fall into their hands by my folly, nor give them any occasion of triumphing over me". Gill spreads the way across providence, grace and duty; Ellicott adds that the word for enemies has been rendered "malignant liers in wait".

On being given over, Clarke presses the Hebrew: it is to their soul, since "their whole soul thirsts for my destruction." Gill ranks three deliverances: it is "a dreadful thing for a man to be given up to his own heart's lusts", worse to fall into Satan's hands, grievous to fall among men "whose tender mercies are cruel".

Verse 13 is the chapter's textual crux, and the three who face it propose three different remedies. Delitzsch holds a word is missing: joined to the preceding verse the sentence "trails badly after it", so "the apodosis is wanting to the protasis" — a word "indispensably necessary", attested by the Greek and the Targum alone. Clarke reaches the opposite conclusion from the same gap. The words "I had fainted" are supplied by the translators, and "far from being necessary, they injure the sense": throw them out, "leave a break after the verse, and the elegant figure of the psalmist will be preserved" — "unless I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living" — what, alas! should have become of me! The figure has a name, aposiopesis, "an abrupt breaking off in the midst of a speech", whose counterpart Clarke finds in Neptune's unfinished threat to the winds that scattered the fleet of Aeneas. Ellicott takes a third road, textual rather than rhetorical: "by slightly changing a letter, we avoid the awkward ellipse", yielding "so that I did not believe to see".

Where the others argue syntax, Spurgeon and Gill take the fainting as fact. Spurgeon notes it is "a common infirmity; even he who slew Goliath was subject to its attacks", and prescribes: "faith puts its bottle of cordial to the lip of the soul, and so prevents fainting." He turns the two verbs into a rule — "we must believe to see, not see to believe" — and reverses the phrase: "in this land of the dying, it is our blessedness to be looking and longing for our fair portion in the land of the living". Gill catalogues the occasions of fainting: the continuance of afflictions, the fear that they come in wrath, "the hidings of God's face".

The closing exhortation is read as spoken out of what precedes. Gill takes it as addressed "either to himself or to others, or it may be to both", and lists what waiting means — as servants who "observe his orders", as beggars who "take repulses and wait". Clarke makes David the example rather than the exhorter: "take me for an example. I waited on him, and he strengthened my heart; wait ye on him, and he will strengthen your heart" — and borrows the Vulgate's act like a man. Spurgeon builds the word into four postures: "wait at his door with prayer; wait at his foot with humility; wait at his table with service; wait at his window with expectancy" — "suitors often win nothing but the cold shoulder from earthly patrons; he speeds best whose patron is in the skies." Of the strengthening he says God "can lay the plaister right upon the weak place", since "a strong heart makes a strong arm". Ellicott corrects both halves: better "let thy heart be strong", and the doubled command is simply "wait for Jehovah, and wait for Jehovah".
